claim: Vernalization is a requirement for prolonged cold to trigger flowering that aligns reproductive development with favorable spring conditions.
source: The requirement for vernalization, a need for prolonged cold to trigger flowering, aligns reproductive development with favorable spring conditions.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about vernalization that represents established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: In Arabidopsis thaliana, vernalization depends on the cold-induced epigenetic silencing of the floral repressor locus FLC.
source: In Arabidopsis thaliana vernalization depends on the cold-induced epigenetic silencing of the floral repressor locus FLC.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Michaels and Amasino, 1999; Sheldon et al., 1999) in the Introduction section.

claim: Extensive natural variation in vernalization response is associated with A. thaliana accessions collected from different geographical regions.
source: Extensive natural variation in vernalization response is associated with A. thaliana accessions collected from different geographical regions.
evidence: This is supported by the study's analysis of multiple accessions from different locations and by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Vernalization required temperatures above 0°C in all the accessions tested.
source: Vernalization required temperatures above 0°C and was still relatively effective at 14°C in all the accessions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 where all genotypes showed limited vernalization at 0°C.

claim: Vernalization was still relatively effective at 14°C in all the accessions tested.
source: Vernalization required temperatures above 0°C and was still relatively effective at 14°C in all the accessions.
evidence: This is supported by experimental flowering time data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Different accessions had characteristic vernalization temperature profiles.
source: The different accessions had characteristic vernalization temperature profiles.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data in Figure 1 showing distinct temperature response patterns for each accession.

claim: One Northern Swedish accession (Lov-1) showed maximum vernalization at 8°C at the level of flowering time.
source: One Northern Swedish accession showed maximum vernalization at 8°C, both at the level of flowering time and FLC chromatin silencing.
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data in Figure 1B and expression/chromatin data in Figure 2.

claim: One Northern Swedish accession (Lov-1) showed maximum vernalization at 8°C at the level of FLC chromatin silencing.
source: One Northern Swedish accession showed maximum vernalization at 8°C, both at the level of flowering time and FLC chromatin silencing.
evidence: This is supported by H3K27me3 ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Historical temperature records predicted all accessions would vernalize in autumn in N. Sweden.
source: Historical temperature records predicted all accessions would vernalize in autumn in N. Sweden, a prediction we validated in field transplantation experiments.
evidence: This is supported by climate data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Field transplantation experiments validated that all accessions vernalize in autumn in N. Sweden.
source: Historical temperature records predicted all accessions would vernalize in autumn in N. Sweden, a prediction we validated in field transplantation experiments.
evidence: This is supported by field experiment data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The vernalization response of different accessions in the field matched that when the average field temperature was given as a constant condition.
source: The vernalization response of the different accessions was monitored over three intervals in the field and found to match that when the average field temperature was given as a constant condition.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the comparison data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The vernalization temperature range of 0–14°C meant all accessions fully vernalized before snowfall in N. Sweden.
source: The vernalization temperature range of 0–14°C meant all accessions fully vernalized before snowfall in N. Sweden.
evidence: This is supported by field experiment data (Figure 3B) and climate data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) showing autumn temperatures fall within this range.

claim: Cold exposure promotes a cell-autonomous epigenetic switch at FLC in an increasing proportion of cells.
source: Cold exposure promotes a cell-autonomous epigenetic switch at FLC in an increasing proportion of cells (Angel et al., 2011, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by Angel et al.

claim: The epigenetic switching mechanism at FLC requires a Polycomb complex associated with PHD proteins.
source: This epigenetic switching mechanism requires a Polycomb complex associated with PHD proteins (De Lucia et al., 2008), including the cold-induced VIN3 (Sung and Amasino, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The epigenetic switching mechanism at FLC includes the cold-induced VIN3 protein.
source: This epigenetic switching mechanism requires a Polycomb complex associated with PHD proteins (De Lucia et al., 2008), including the cold-induced VIN3 (Sung and Amasino, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sung and Amasino, 2004.

claim: Epigenetic silencing of FLC enables activation of FT.
source: This enables activation of FT, is a potent activator of flowering in A. thaliana (Searle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Searle et al., 2006.

claim: FT is a potent activator of flowering in A. thaliana.
source: This enables activation of FT, is a potent activator of flowering in A. thaliana (Searle et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Searle et al., 2006.

claim: At a standard vernalization temperature of 5°C, the length of cold required to achieve complete epigenetic silencing varies between A. thaliana accessions.
source: At a standard vernalization temperature of 5°C, the length of cold required to achieve complete epigenetic silencing varies between A. thaliana accessions and this maps to non-coding cis polymorphisms in FLC (Coustham et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Variation in the length of cold required to achieve complete epigenetic silencing maps to non-coding cis polymorphisms in FLC.
source: At a standard vernalization temperature of 5°C, the length of cold required to achieve complete epigenetic silencing varies between A. thaliana accessions and this maps to non-coding cis polymorphisms in FLC (Coustham et al., 2012; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Coustham et al., 2012 and Li et al., 2014.

claim: Accessions collected from northerly latitudes typically require longer vernalization.
source: Accessions collected from northerly latitudes typically require longer vernalization, for example, the accession Lov-1 originates from near the northerly limit of the Arabidopsis range in Lövvik, North Sweden (62.5°N) and requires three months of vernalization to fully accelerate flowering (Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations and by the example of Lov-1.

claim: The accession Lov-1 originates from near the northerly limit of the Arabidopsis range in Lövvik, North Sweden (62.5°N).
source: Accessions collected from northerly latitudes typically require longer vernalization, for example, the accession Lov-1 originates from near the northerly limit of the Arabidopsis range in Lövvik, North Sweden (62.5°N) and requires three months of vernalization to fully accelerate flowering (Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the geographic origin of the accession.

claim: Lov-1 requires three months of vernalization to fully accelerate flowering.
source: Accessions collected from northerly latitudes typically require longer vernalization, for example, the accession Lov-1 originates from near the northerly limit of the Arabidopsis range in Lövvik, North Sweden (62.5°N) and requires three months of vernalization to fully accelerate flowering (Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shindo et al., 2006 and Coustham et al., 2012.

claim: A genetically informed photothermal model for flowering in A. thaliana has assumed that vernalization occurs when daytime hourly temperatures are higher than 0°C and lower than 6°C.
source: A genetically informed photothermal model for flowering in A. thaliana has assumed that vernalization occurs when daytime hourly temperatures are higher than 0°C and lower than 6°C (Wilczek et al., 2009; Chew et al., 2012, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: Accessions from southern Europe have been found to vernalize at constant temperatures significantly higher than 6°C.
source: However, accessions from southern Europe have been found to vernalize at constant temperatures significantly higher than 6°C (Wollenberg and Amasino, 2012), suggesting that accessions from northerly latitudes might vernalize most efficiently at relatively low temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wollenberg and Amasino, 2012.

claim: All genotypes showed limited vernalization after 4 and 6 weeks exposure to 0°C.
source: All the genotypes showed limited vernalization after 4 and 6 weeks exposure to 0°C and vernalized more efficiently at all other temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1A-E.

claim: All genotypes vernalized more efficiently at temperatures above 0°C than at 0°C.
source: All the genotypes showed limited vernalization after 4 and 6 weeks exposure to 0°C and vernalized more efficiently at all other temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1A-E.

claim: Col FRISf2 was most effectively vernalized after 4, 6 or 12 weeks at 2°C, 5°C and 8°C.
source: Col FRISf2 and Edi-0 were most effectively vernalized after 4, 6 or 12 weeks at 2°C, 5°C and 8°C and still vernalized relatively efficiently at 12°C and 14°C (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Edi-0 was most effectively vernalized after 4, 6 or 12 weeks at 2°C, 5°C and 8°C.
source: Col FRISf2 and Edi-0 were most effectively vernalized after 4, 6 or 12 weeks at 2°C, 5°C and 8°C and still vernalized relatively efficiently at 12°C and 14°C (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Col FRISf2 and Edi-0 still vernalized relatively efficiently at 12°C and 14°C.
source: Col FRISf2 and Edi-0 were most effectively vernalized after 4, 6 or 12 weeks at 2°C, 5°C and 8°C and still vernalized relatively efficiently at 12°C and 14°C (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: After 2 weeks of cold at 2°C and 8°C, the flowering of Col FRISf2 plants was similar.
source: Even after 2 weeks of cold at 2°C and 8°C the flowering of Col FRISf2 plants was similar, so lack of any difference was not due to vernalization being close to saturation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ull2-5 showed similar temperature sensitivity to Col FRISf2 and Edi-0, but required 12 weeks for vernalization to be fully effective.
source: Ull2-5 showed similar temperature sensitivity to Col FRISf2 and Edi-0, but required 12 weeks for vernalization to be fully effective (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Lov-1 and Var2-6 plants showed a differential response to temperature with 2 and 12°C less effective than 5 and 8°C after 6-weeks vernalization.
source: In contrast, Lov-1 and Var2-6 plants showed a differential response to temperature with 2 and 12°C less effective than 5 and 8°C after 6-weeks vernalization (Figure 1B and E).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1B and E.

claim: For Lov-1, the only temperature that resulted in flowering after 4 weeks exposure was 8°C.
source: For Lov-1 the only temperature that resulted in flowering after 4 weeks exposure was 8°C and although the enhanced effect of this temperature diminished over time, 8°C consistently resulted in the most effective vernalization (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: For Lov-1, 8°C consistently resulted in the most effective vernalization.
source: For Lov-1 the only temperature that resulted in flowering after 4 weeks exposure was 8°C and although the enhanced effect of this temperature diminished over time, 8°C consistently resulted in the most effective vernalization (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The requirement for longer cold for effective vernalization in the Lov-1 accession involves quantitative variation in accumulation of epigenetic silencing of FLC.
source: The requirement for longer cold for effective vernalization in the Lov-1 accession has previously been shown to involve quantitative variation in accumulation of epigenetic silencing of FLC (Shindo et al., 2006; Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The Lov-1 FLC allele re-activated after 30 days in the warm after vernalization at all the tested temperatures.
source: In contrast to Col FRISf2, the Lov-1 allele re-activated after 30 days in the warm after vernalization at all the tested temperatures.
evidence: This is supported by FLC expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The degree of FLC re-activation in Lov-1 was lowest after vernalization at 8°C.
source: However, the degree of re-activation was lowest after vernalization at 8°C, consistent with vernalization being most effective at this temperature.
evidence: This is supported by FLC expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: 6 weeks vernalization at 8°C resulted in lower FLC re-activation post-cold than 5°C in Lov-1.
source: Similarly, 6 weeks vernalization at 8°C resulted in lower FLC re-activation post-cold and higher levels of FT induction than 5°C, with similar VIN3 expression (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 6 weeks vernalization at 8°C resulted in higher levels of FT induction than 5°C in Lov-1.
source: Similarly, 6 weeks vernalization at 8°C resulted in lower FLC re-activation post-cold and higher levels of FT induction than 5°C, with similar VIN3 expression (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: VIN3 expression was similar after 6 weeks vernalization at 8°C and 5°C in Lov-1.
source: Similarly, 6 weeks vernalization at 8°C resulted in lower FLC re-activation post-cold and higher levels of FT induction than 5°C, with similar VIN3 expression (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by expression data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Epigenetic silencing of FLC is associated with Polycomb silencing and accumulation of H3K27me3 over the gene body.
source: Epigenetic silencing of FLC is associated with Polycomb silencing and accumulation of H3K27me3 over the gene body (Angel et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In Lov-1, it takes longer to accumulate H3K27me3 at FLC, mainly due to lower starting levels.
source: In Lov-1 it takes longer to accumulate the H3K27me3, mainly due to lower starting levels (Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coustham et al., 2012.

claim: Similar accumulation of gene body H3K27me3 occurred in the Col FRISf2 FLC allele at 5, 8 or 14°C.
source: We found similar accumulation of gene body H3K27me3 in the Col FRISf2 FLC allele at 5, 8 or 14°C, but differential H3K27me3 accumulation in the Lov-1 allele (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Differential H3K27me3 accumulation occurred in the Lov-1 FLC allele at different temperatures.
source: We found similar accumulation of gene body H3K27me3 in the Col FRISf2 FLC allele at 5, 8 or 14°C, but differential H3K27me3 accumulation in the Lov-1 allele (Figure 2D, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Vernalization at 8°C resulted in higher levels of H3K27me3 compared to 5 or 14°C in Lov-1.
source: Vernalization at 8°C resulted in higher levels of H3K27me3 compared to 5 or 14°C (Figure 2D), suggesting that the Polycomb silencing is most effective at 8°C for the Lov-1 FLC allele.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Polycomb silencing is most effective at 8°C for the Lov-1 FLC allele.
source: Vernalization at 8°C resulted in higher levels of H3K27me3 compared to 5 or 14°C (Figure 2D), suggesting that the Polycomb silencing is most effective at 8°C for the Lov-1 FLC allele.
evidence: This is inferred from the H3K27me3 ChIP data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Flower buds appeared within 2 weeks of the snowmelt on native Arabidopsis at the N. Swedish Lövvik site.
source: The relatively high temperature range for vernalization of the N. Swedish accession was surprising given that flower buds appeared within 2 weeks of the snowmelt on native Arabidopsis at the N. Swedish Lövvik site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by photographic evidence shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Early flowering may limit herbivory and help in the competition for nutrients.
source: This early flowering may limit herbivory and help in the competition for nutrients (Kawagoe and Kudoh, 2010; Akiyama and Agren, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A long-term (>5 year study) of the natural populations at several N. Swedish sites showed most populations behaved as winter annuals with germination occurring predominantly in August and September with no spring germination.
source: A long-term (>5 year study) of the natural populations at several N. Swedish sites throughout the High Coast region, showed most populations behaved as winter annuals with germination occurring predominantly in August and September with no spring germination (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by observational data collected over multiple years.

claim: Vernalization must have occurred before the end of November given the recurrent snow cover and low temperatures at the Lövvik site over the winter months.
source: The rapid flowering after snowmelt suggests that vernalization must have occurred before the end of November given the recurrent snow cover and low temperatures at the Lövvik site over the winter months (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from the rapid flowering observation combined with climate data.

claim: Hourly climate data collected near Lövvik between 1st August and snow cover between 2008 and 2013 show an average air temperature of ~8°C.
source: Hourly climate data collected near Lövvik between 1st August (the earliest germination date observed for natural populations) until snow cover between 2008 and 2013 show an average air temperature of ~8°C (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by climate data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Analysis of national data (1st August—30th November) revealed an overall average autumn daily average temperature of 8.86°C between 1961 and 2008 (SD = 0.63).
source: Analysis of national data (1st August—30th November) also revealed an overall average autumn daily average temperature of 8.86°C between 1961 and 2008 (SD = 0.63) with over 86% of days falling within the range identified as being effective for Lov-1 vernalization, (0°C, 15°C) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by historical climate data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Over 86% of days between 1961 and 2008 (1st August—30th November) fell within the range identified as being effective for Lov-1 vernalization (0°C, 15°C).
source: Analysis of national data (1st August—30th November) also revealed an overall average autumn daily average temperature of 8.86°C between 1961 and 2008 (SD = 0.63) with over 86% of days falling within the range identified as being effective for Lov-1 vernalization, (0°C, 15°C) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by historical climate data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Vernalization was complete by the end of November in both 2011 and 2012 in field experiments.
source: Flowering time of the different cohorts showed that vernalization was complete by the end of November in both 2011 (Figure 3B) and 2012 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by flowering time data from field experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Plants left to overwinter in the field flowered rapidly at snowmelt, at the same time as the native A. thaliana population.
source: Furthermore, plants left to overwinter in the field flowered rapidly at snowmelt, at the same time as the native A. thaliana population (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by field observation data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: The optimal vernalizing temperature for Lov-1 matched the average temperature over the 3-month season when vernalization occurred.
source: It was therefore interesting that the optimal vernalizing temperature for Lov-1 matched the average temperature over the 3-month season when vernalization occurred (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the optimal temperature (8°C) with the average field temperature data.

claim: Expression analysis in the perennial species Arabidopsis halleri growing under natural field conditions has shown that plants average temperature over long-term scales.
source: Expression analysis in the perennial species Arabidopsis halleri growing under natural field conditions has shown that plants average temperature over long-term scales (Aikawa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aikawa et al., 2010.

claim: Different genotypes showed temporal differences in vernalization responsiveness over the three transplant periods in the field.
source: The different genotypes showed temporal differences in vernalization responsiveness over the three transplant periods in the field.
evidence: This is supported by field experiment data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Vernalization responsiveness was very similar when the average field temperature was given as a constant temperature, with each genotype showing a different overall profile.
source: Remarkably, vernalization responsiveness was very similar when the average field temperature was given as a constant temperature, with each genotype showing a different overall profile (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison data shown in Figure 4.

claim: All the genotypes analysed were found to vernalize effectively during autumn.
source: All the genotypes analysed were found to vernalize effectively during autumn (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), however they have been shown to differ in their seed dormancy (Atwell et al., 2010); accessions from N. Sweden generally have much lower seed dormancy requirement than those from further south (Debieu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by field experiment data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: Genotypes differ in their seed dormancy.
source: All the genotypes analysed were found to vernalize effectively during autumn (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), however they have been shown to differ in their seed dormancy (Atwell et al., 2010); accessions from N. Sweden generally have much lower seed dormancy requirement than those from further south (Debieu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Accessions from N. Sweden generally have much lower seed dormancy requirement than those from further south.
source: All the genotypes analysed were found to vernalize effectively during autumn (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 5B), however they have been shown to differ in their seed dormancy (Atwell et al., 2010); accessions from N. Sweden generally have much lower seed dormancy requirement than those from further south (Debieu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Debieu et al., 2013.

claim: The low seed dormancy of Lov-1 would enable germination to occur early enough to exploit the whole of the N. Swedish autumn for vernalization.
source: Thus, the low seed dormancy of Lov-1 would enable germination to occur early enough to exploit the whole of the N. Swedish autumn for vernalization.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of seed dormancy data and field observations.

claim: The increased seed dormancy of S. Swedish accessions (e.g., Ull2-5) is likely to delay germination leading to the necessity for vernalization in some years to extend into winter in S. Sweden.
source: The increased seed dormancy of S. Swedish accessions (e.g., Ull2-5) is likely to delay germination leading to the necessity for vernalization in some years to extend into winter in S. Sweden.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on seed dormancy differences.

claim: The reduced effectiveness of temperatures below 5°C for Swedish accessions Lov-1 and Var2-6 could prevent premature vernalization occurring during unseasonal cool periods in early autumn.
source: It is interesting to speculate that the reduced effectiveness of temperatures below 5°C for other Swedish accessions Lov-1 and Var2-6 (Figure 1B,E) could prevent premature vernalization occurring during unseasonal cool periods in early autumn.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: The (0°C, 6°C) temperature range widely used to estimate vernalization in A. thaliana would only predict partial vernalization of later flowering accessions during the field experiments.
source: Our data also show that the (0°C, 6°C) temperature range widely used to estimate vernalization in A. thaliana (Wilczek et al., 2009) would only predict partial vernalization of later flowering accessions during our field experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the model predictions with actual field data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Raising the upper threshold temperature to 15°C would improve estimates of vernalization progress for later flowering accessions under natural field conditions.
source: Our data suggest that raising the upper threshold temperature to 15°C would improve estimates of vernalization progress for later flowering accessions under natural field conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing effective vernalization at temperatures up to 14°C.

claim: Growth at the northern limit of the A. thaliana species range has involved a seasonal shift in the timing of vernalization.
source: In summary, we have employed a combination of molecular and ecological approaches to connect temperature-induced molecular changes at FLC with ecologically significant effects in the field. We show that growth at the northern limit of the A. thaliana species range has involved a seasonal shift in the timing of vernalization.
evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by the combined field and molecular data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: One N. Swedish accession, Lov-1, shows a more distinct vernalization temperature optimum that matches the average historical temperature for August-November in that geographical region.
source: Perhaps as a response to selection in these extreme conditions one N. Swedish accession, Lov-1, shows a more distinct vernalization temperature optimum that matches the average historical temperature for August-November in that geographical region (Figure 1, Figure 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data (Figures 1 and 2) and climate data (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).

claim: Early germination enables vernalization to complete before snowfall and allows flowering to occur directly after snowmelt when the photoperiod and ambient temperatures increase.
source: Early germination enables vernalization to complete before snowfall and allows flowering to occur directly after snowmelt when the photoperiod and ambient temperatures increase.
evidence: This is inferred from the field observations and germination timing data.

claim: Rises in global temperature have already reduced vernalization periods to an extent that has impacted the phenology of a range of plant species.
source: Rises in global temperature have already reduced vernalization periods to an extent that has impacted the phenology of a range of plant species (Fitter and Fitter, 2002; Cook et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on climate change impacts.

claim: NILLov-1 took longer to flower than Col FRISf2 after the first two transfers in 2012.
source: NILLov-1 took longer to flower than Col FRISf2 after the first two transfers in 2012 (Figure 3—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This is supported by field experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The Lov-1 FLC allele contributes to differential vernalization response under field conditions.
source: This revealed the clear contribution of the Lov-1 FLC allele to differential vernalization response under field conditions, which likely involves the four non-coding polymorphisms in FLC close to the nucleation site of the PHD-PRC2 previously defined as underpinning the molecular variation in FLC epigenetic silencing between Lov-1 and Col FRISf2 (Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the NIL experiment data and supported by citation to previous molecular work.

claim: The differential vernalization response likely involves four non-coding polymorphisms in FLC close to the nucleation site of the PHD-PRC2.
source: This revealed the clear contribution of the Lov-1 FLC allele to differential vernalization response under field conditions, which likely involves the four non-coding polymorphisms in FLC close to the nucleation site of the PHD-PRC2 previously defined as underpinning the molecular variation in FLC epigenetic silencing between Lov-1 and Col FRISf2 (Coustham et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coustham et al., 2012 and inferred from the NIL experiment.

claim: The selected genotypes represent most of the major FLC haplotypes.
source: In order to investigate natural variation for vernalization temperature requirement in A. thaliana accessions we selected several genotypes that represent most of the major FLC haplotypes (Li et al., 2014): Lov-1 (Lövvik, N. Sweden—latitude 62.5°N), Var2-6 (Vårhallen, S. Sweden—latitude 55.58°N), Ull2-5 (Ullstorp, S. Sweden—latitude 56.06°N), Edi-0 (Edinburgh, UK—latitude 55.95°N) and the reference Columbia line containing FRIGIDA (Col FRISf2, [Michaels and Amasino, 1999]) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2014.
